title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: A person in motion always invents a purpose for that motion. To be able to go a thousand miles, you must imagine that something good awaits you at the end of those thousand miles. You need the prospect of a promised land to have the strength to keep moving.

For the French during their advance, the promised land had been Moscow. During their retreat, it was their homeland. But their homeland was too far away, and for someone traveling a thousand miles, it's absolutely necessary to set aside the final goal and say to himself: 'Today I'll reach a place twenty-five miles ahead, where I'll rest and spend the night.' And during that first day's journey, the resting place eclipses the ultimate destination and draws all your hopes and desires. The impulses felt by a single person are always magnified in a crowd.

For the French retreating along the old Smolensk road, the final goal—their homeland—was too remote. Their immediate goal was Smolensk, toward which all their desires and hopes, enormously intensified in the mass, propelled them onward. It wasn't that they knew plenty of food and fresh troops awaited them in Smolensk, nor were they told so (on the contrary, their superior officers, and Napoleon himself, knew that provisions there were scarce). But this was the only thing that could give them the strength to keep moving and endure their present privations. So those who knew and those who didn't both deceived themselves and pushed on toward Smolensk as toward a promised land.

Reaching the highway, the French fled with astonishing energy and unheard-of speed toward their chosen goal. Besides the shared impulse that bound the whole crowd of French into one mass and gave it a kind of energy, there was another cause binding them together: their sheer numbers. As with the physical law of gravity, their enormous mass drew individual human atoms to itself. In their hundreds of thousands, they moved like an entire nation.

Each man wanted nothing more than to give himself up as a prisoner and escape the horror and misery. But on one hand, the force of this common attraction to Smolensk, their goal, drew every one of them in the same direction; on the other, an army corps can't surrender to a company. Though the French availed themselves of every convenient opportunity to break away and surrender on the slightest decent pretext, such pretexts did not always occur. Their very numbers and their crowded and swift movement deprived them of that possibility and made it not just difficult but impossible for the Russians to stop this movement, to which the French were directing all their energies. Beyond a certain limit, no mechanical disruption of the body could hasten the process of decomposition.

A lump of snow can't be melted all at once. There is a minimum time required, and no amount of heat can melt it faster. On the contrary, the more heat you apply, the harder the remaining snow becomes.

Of the Russian commanders, Kutuzov alone understood this. When the flight of the French army along the Smolensk road became well defined, what Konovnitsyn had foreseen on the night of the eleventh of October began to happen. Every senior officer wanted to distinguish himself—to cut off, seize, capture, and overthrow the French—and all clamored for action.
Kutuzov alone used all his power (and a commander in chief's power is very limited) to prevent an attack.

He couldn't tell them what we say now: 'Why fight? Why block the road, losing our own men and inhumanely slaughtering miserable wretches? What's the point, when a third of their army has melted away on the road from Moscow to Vyazma without any battle?' But drawing on his years of wisdom, he told them what they could understand—about the golden bridge, the old idea of leaving a beaten enemy an open road rather than cornering it—and they laughed at him and slandered him, flinging themselves on, tearing at, and gloating over the dying beast.

Ermolov, Miloradovich, Platov, and others near the French at Vyazma couldn't resist their desire to cut off and smash two French corps. To inform Kutuzov of their intentions, they sent him a blank sheet of paper in an envelope.

And try as Kutuzov might to hold the troops back, our men attacked, trying to block the road. Infantry regiments, we are told, advanced to the attack with music playing and drums beating, and killed and lost thousands of men.
But they didn't cut off or overthrow anyone. The French army, closing ranks more tightly in the face of danger, continued, while steadily melting away, to pursue its fatal path toward Smolensk.
